correctness.rationale: The cyclic matching-polynomial identity follows from closed transfer-matrix paths. All six products share determinant \(s^6\prod f_j\), and the Perron root is strictly monotone in trace. The exhaustive exact integer certificate checks all 720 six-rank permutations and 60 dihedral classes, with unique statistics extrema. It follows algebraically that A/B differ by \(s^2p^2d^2(-1+2sd/p^2)\) and C maximizes all positive-variable terms. Matching polynomials of cycles shorter than six have at most two dimers and cannot change pairwise order as common survival parameters vary. Exact rational checker verifies 720 direct 2x2 products against the derived polynomial under four distinct parameter settings and validates the complete finite orbit table. No sampled parameters substitute for the all-real proof.

originality.rationale: Originality passes within actually inspected literature and published-claim comparisons, provisionally. The specific finite six-level fertility-calendar optimizer, its sharp \(sd=p^2/2\) minimizer transition, stable maximizer and minimal-calendar-length theorem were not implied by inspected source results. Periodic growth and cyclic continuants are established prior concepts; inaccessible technical primary texts and unsearched generalizations leave historical-priority risk.

Broad generalized cyclic-continuant and transfer-matrix rearrangement results may exist and imply this special six-step theorem without using the same ecological terminology.
Published-claim searches and historical overlap checks are not proof of novelty; independent historical-priority review has not occurred.

value.rationale: The finite complete classification resolves the natural fixed-inventory calendar ordering question for a two-stage population and identifies a parameter-dependent shift in worst-case long-run growth, while establishing that six is the minimum possible length for any such shift. The exact threshold, independent of baseline fertility, can guide theoretical counterexamples and tests of naive season-order invariance. This is a structural theoretical result with no empirical or management-effect assertion.
